cases.title: Novi Sad Railway Station: Canopy Collapse on the China Exim-Financed Line

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Lent to the Serbian government under agreements of May 2017 and April 2019 that parliament adopted, for the first two sections of a railway modernisation costing about US$1.5 billion in total (CHOICE). The Exim share is not stated. The final section went to Russia's state railway company on a Russian loan.

cases.conditions: The Chinese consortium was selected before the loan agreements were final, under a July 2018 commercial contract covering the Novi Sad–Subotica section, which includes the station. CHOICE says such contracts were not accessible, while linking an archived copy of this one.

companies.name: China Railway International and China Communications Construction Company (CRIC-CCCC)
companies.role: Consortium that carried out the station reconstruction, 2021 to mid-2024 (Wikipedia; Latin Times); hired the Serbian subcontractor Starting for the rooftop work (CHOICE). Two of the 13 defendants are accused over work for the consortium (Vreme).

cases.community: The station reopened on 5 July 2024. On 1 November 2024 its concrete front canopy fell. Sixteen people died: 14 at the scene, Anja Radonjić, 24, in hospital in November 2024 and Vukašin Crnčević, 18, on 21 March 2025. One survivor was left with severe injuries (Srpske; Vreme).
cases.suppression: On the night of 27–28 January 2025 four ruling-party activists assaulted students in Novi Sad, breaking a female student's jaw. The president pardoned the four in July 2025, before any verdict (N1).
cases.killed_note: Not counted: 16 people died, but as of 1 November 2026 no court has ruled on the cause and no one has been held responsible by a final verdict (Srpske). Prosecutors argue corrosion at the joint between tie rod and roof beam, plus added elements that overloaded the structure. Faculty of Technical Sciences experts say the canopy would have collapsed even without the reconstruction, because of corroded tension rods; other engineers blame weight added in the work (Wikipedia). An independent expert panel said work was rushed under political pressure (Latin Times). The consortium says the canopy had only conservation work.
cases.outcome: Prosecutors indicted 13 people, including former minister Goran Vesić, who denies responsibility. On 24 December 2025 the Novi Sad High Court dropped charges against Vesić and five others; in June 2026 the Court of Appeal reversed that, so all 13 face trial (N1; Vreme). As of 1 November 2026 no trial had begun, because defence motions are at the Supreme Court. Organized-crime prosecutors are separately investigating about US$115 million in alleged budget damage on the Novi Sad–Kelebija section (Srpske). Prime Minister Miloš Vučević resigned on 28 January 2025 (Al Jazeera).

The Novi Sad Railway Station Collapse: The Cost of Sino-Serbian Infrastructure Deals
sources.publisher: China Observers in Central and Eastern Europe (CHOICE)

sources.title: Serbia: Gov't criticised for lack of transparency and accountability in Chinese Consortium's railway project following the roof collapse
Appeals court confirms indictment for Novi Sad Railway Station tragedy
The "Canopy" case: What are the defendants accused of?
Defense of the former minister: What Goran Vesić told the prosecution about the canopy
Two Years Since the Novi Sad Station Canopy Collapse
Two Years After Novi Sad's Train Station Deadly Canopy Collapse, Serbia Mourns Amid New Political Hope

cases.confidence_note: China Exim's loans are documented, but the Exim share of the cost is not stated. CRIC-CCCC and Serbian Railways Infrastructure say the canopy was not reconstructed and got only conservation work; social media later showed workers repairing its tiles (Wikipedia). The cause is unsettled: an indictment is an accusation, and the experts disagree on whether old corrosion or the renovation mattered more.

lvwhy.project: The station was rebuilt under the railway project.
lvwhy.finance: China Exim loans paid for the line.

cases.title: Drmno Village Between the Kostolac Plant and Its China Exim-Financed Mine Expansion

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: US$293 million signed 29 December 2011 for upgrades to Kostolac B1 and B2, a desulphurisation unit, a Danube dock and rail; US$608 million signed December 2014 for the new B3 unit and the Drmno mine expansion (Bankwatch).

cases.conditions: An intergovernmental agreement exempted joint projects from tenders, so CMEC was chosen without one. Parliament ratified the second loan on 19 January 2015 in a session announced less than 24 hours earlier; disputes go to arbitration in Beijing (Bankwatch).

companies.name: China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC)
companies.role: Builder of the Kostolac works and mine expansion (Bankwatch)

cases.community: Mine capacity is rising from 9–10 million to 12 million tonnes a year. Bankwatch says Drmno is hemmed into about 20 square km between the plant, the mine and a new dock. A 2016 survey commissioned by the NGO CEKOR covered 162 of 246 households and described health problems and house cracks in a large majority. Residents showed cracks they attribute to mining vibration and medical records of worsening health; some have moved abroad. A petition signed by most villagers asked for resettlement, which has not been offered (Bankwatch, 2019).
cases.ecosystem: Sulphur dioxide from Kostolac B was 1.6 times the allowed level in 2021 and still more than twice the limit in 2024. The desulphurisation unit declared complete in July 2017 began test runs only in October 2022 (Bankwatch).
cases.outcome: EPS said the parish council rejected the petition as illegitimate and did not respond. No impact assessment was required for the mine expansion; the Energy Community Secretariat opened a dispute case in 2021. Administrative courts ruled for CEKOR in 2016 and 2022, and the ministry issued a similar approval almost at once after the second ruling (Bankwatch).

sources.title: Kostolac B3 power plant, Serbia
Serbia is mining away a green future
Serbia: Local residents concerned about rapidly expanding Drmno coal mine
Household survey in Drmno shows negative impacts of Kostolac B3 project, Drmno mine
Serbia power utility EPS on Drmno community

cases.confidence_note: Loans and emissions are documented. House cracks and illness come from Bankwatch and CEKOR, NGOs campaigning on this project, and from residents. EPS says CEKOR's research was not done by accredited institutions, that heart disease and hypertension in Drmno are below the Serbian average (hypertension 18–23% against over 30%), that heating and traffic are major local air polluters, and that no document made resettlement a condition (Environment SEE). The plant is older than the Chinese loans.

lvwhy.project: Loans paid for the mine expansion around the village.
lvwhy.land: The mine has closed in on the village without resettlement.

cases.title: Stanari Coal Plant: China Development Bank Loan and the Raškovci Mine Expansion

lenders.name: China Development Bank
lenders.role: EUR 350 million loan to EFT, out of an estimated EUR 550 million plant cost. If EFT defaults the bank would take over the mining concession and plant (Environment SEE; BIRN Detektor).

cases.conditions: The Republika Srpska government changed its concessions law so EFT could obtain the loan and build the plant (BIRN Detektor).

companies.name: EFT
companies.role: Owner of the plant and mine, which took the loan (BIRN Detektor); its operating company is a subsidiary of UK-headquartered EFT Investments SE (Sarajevo Times)
companies.hq: United Kingdom (EFT Investments SE, per Sarajevo Times)

companies.name: Dongfang
companies.role: Builder of the 300 MW plant, which began commercial operation in September 2016 (Bankwatch)

cases.community: A meter placed at a resident's home near the mine and plant in Stanari recorded up to 828 micrograms of dust per cubic metre in one hour on 17 July 2019 (Center for Environment). Monitoring from 4 July to 1 August 2019 found the 24-hour PM10 limit passed twice (Sarajevo Times). Residents nearest the mine say their health, farmland and home values are falling. Separately, Dario Jerinić says his family must leave its home for the Raškovci mine expansion, excavators 60–70 metres away cracked the walls, about 17,000 square metres of woodland was cut, and EFT wastewater flooded a water source used by several families (BIRN Detektor, 2021).
cases.outcome: Jerinić says police and prosecutors did not act and he could not get a fair settlement for his land. EFT declined to comment. The Republika Srpska ministry says it made no checks for two years and received no complaints; the inspectorate says the sites followed regulations until the pandemic (BIRN Detektor).

sources.title: Bosnia displays lenient attitude to foreign investment in dirty energy
Stanari lignite power plant, Bosnia and Herzegovina
Environmental issues and Chinese capital in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Stanari coal power plant
Alarming levels of dust particles in Stanari
Ecologists warn that Residents around Stanari coal-fired Power Plant are regularly affected by Pollution from different Directions

cases.confidence_note: The loan is documented. The dust readings come from Bankwatch and its partner Center for Environment, and the dust is attributed to the mine and plant together. Lignite has been mined here since 1948 (Environment SEE), though the readings came after the plant opened in 2016. Jerinić's account is one family's, and the article does not say where his home is. Bankwatch notes mixed local reaction.

lvwhy.project: The loan paid for the plant the mine now feeds.
lvwhy.finance: The bank can take the concession if EFT defaults.

cases.title: Gezhouba Shieli Cement Plant and Kodamanov Village
cases.place: Kodamanov village, Shieli District, Kyzylorda, Kazakhstan
cases.point: Shieli cement plant (AidData map link); Kodamanov village is at its edge

lenders.name: China Eximbank and Bank of China
lenders.role: US$129 million syndicated nine-year loan, committed 2017, US$64.5 million from each, to Gezhouba Shieli Cement Company (AidData 70845, 53795).

lenders.name: Sinosure
lenders.role: Political risk insurance covering up to 95% (AidData).

cases.conditions: The loan paid for most of a US$178.03 million plant making about 1 million tons of cement a year, chiefly oil well cement (AidData).

companies.name: China Gezhouba Group
companies.role: State-run owner, holding 70% with its overseas arm; DANAKE Corporation holds 30% (AidData)

cases.community: The plant, inaugurated in December 2018, stands about 500 metres from homes on Makulbekova Street; rules for a first-class hazard site required at least 1,000 metres (Orda; Global Voices). Villagers report air, water and noise pollution, children's respiratory problems and headaches, and harm to cattle and gardens. Layla Tuganbayeva moved about 1,200 km to Pavlodar province; Almas Duisebayev says no one will buy their houses (Global Voices).
cases.outcome: Villagers sued in 2021. The Shieli District Court found the sanitary agency's conclusion unlawful, and the Kyzylorda regional court upheld this in October 2024, ruling the dust harmful to residents' health (Orda). A Health Ministry order of May 2024 allowed smaller protection zones for "historically established" sites, cutting this one to 450 metres, so the plant stays open (Global Voices).

sources.title: How villagers in Kazakhstan fought against a Chinese cement plant and lost
Court Rules Chinese Cement Plant in Qyzylorda Region Harmful to Health
China Eximbank contributes $64.5 million to $129 million syndicated loan for Shieli cement plant (record 70845)
Bank of China contributes $64.5 million to $129 million syndicated loan for Shieli cement plant (record 53795)

cases.confidence_note: Local authorities assessed the air in 2020 and early 2021 and found no harmful levels; villagers say the plant was shut during inspections, and the court found the results unlawful. The plant appealed and lost; no direct company reply to the health claims was found. AidData dates the start of operations to 18 October 2019. About 600 people worked for the plant in 2023, 90% of them local (Global Voices).

lvwhy.project: The loan built the plant 500 metres from homes.
lvwhy.finance: Two Chinese state banks lent with Sinosure cover.

cases.title: Vinh Tan 2 Coal Plant: Dust over the Village and the 2015 Highway Blockade
cases.place: Vinh Tan, Tuy Phong, Binh Thuan, Vietnam

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: RMB 600 million concessional loan, US$300 million preferential buyer's credit and US$695 million buyer's credit, signed with Vietnam Electricity on 17 December 2010, covering 85% of a US$1.265 billion contract (AidData 65949).

cases.conditions: EVN on-lent the money to its subsidiary Power Generation Corporation 3 and paid Shanghai Electric as main contractor (AidData).
cases.community: Coal ash dust affected about 1,370 nearby households, and residents reported respiratory disease after the plant began running, according to Tuy Phong district authorities (VTV, July 2015). Residents said dust covered homes and fields (AsiaNews; RFA).
cases.suppression: On 14–15 April 2015 villagers blocked Highway 1A, causing a jam of about 20 km. RFA reports thousands of protesters; AsiaNews reports hundreds. Riot police responded. Officials said at least 10 officers were hurt by stones and Molotov cocktails, which AsiaNews could not confirm independently.
cases.outcome: The government had already fined the plant (RFA). The deputy prime minister demanded immediate action from EVN (RFA; AsiaNews). In July 2015, after dust returned, the provincial chairman ordered work toward a temporary halt of Generator 2 and regular inspections (VTV).

cases.title: Neelum-Jhelum Hydropower: River Diverted Past Muzaffarabad
cases.place: Muzaffarabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Pakistan
cases.point: Muzaffarabad city, where the diverted Neelum runs low

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: US$448 million buyer's credit signed in May 2013, repaid through electricity surcharges; AidData also records a US$576 million loan signed in 2016 (AidData 35266).

cases.conditions: The loan was on-lent at 12% to the WAPDA subsidiary building the 969 MW plant, which sends the Neelum through a 32.5 km tunnel to the Jhelum (AidData).

companies.name: China Gezhouba Group (CGGC)
companies.role: Main contractor, in consortium with CMEC (AidData)

companies.name: China National Machinery Import & Export Corporation (CMEC)
companies.role: Main contractor, in consortium with CGGC (AidData)

cases.community: State officials say summer average temperatures in and around Muzaffarabad, a city of more than 190,000, have risen 4–5°C since the river was diverted in 2018, and a local environment official says its heat-absorbing capacity from May to August has more than halved (Reuters). Reuters also reports water shortages. In Chandra village, a resident blames the tunnel for drying up springs; nearly 30% of villagers sold livestock and left, and those remaining pay about PKR 7,000 for 4,000 litres of water (Dialogue Earth).
cases.ecosystem: About 80% of the river's flow was diverted (Reuters). Sewage and waste build up in the riverbed, which Reuters calls a long-standing problem.
cases.outcome: After citizen protests, WAPDA gave funds in 2019 for water and waste schemes and more than three dozen were carried out, but a solid waste plant was never built and the local environment agency withheld its compliance certificate (Reuters). A tunnel blockage forced a shutdown in July 2022 (AidData).

sources.title: Hydropower push leaves Pakistani Kashmir's capital hot and bothered
Protests bring CPEC's Kashmir dam to a halt
China Eximbank provides $448 million buyer's credit loan for 969MW Neelum-Jhelum Hydroelectric Project (record 35266)
969-MW Neelum Jhelum hydropower project gets boost from China Exim

cases.confidence_note: The temperature figures come from officials and have not been separated from wider warming. Residents also say India's Kishanganga project reduced the water reaching the city, which India denies (Dialogue Earth). Construction began in 2008, before the Chinese loan, but the harm began with the 2018 diversion.

lvwhy.project: The tunnel took the river away from the city and nearby springs.
lvwhy.finance: China Exim lent, repaid through electricity surcharges.

cases.title: Sahiwal Coal Plant: Falling Water and Crop Losses Reported at Qadirabad
cases.place: Qadirabad and Chak 76/5R, Sahiwal, Punjab, Pakistan
cases.point: Sahiwal coal plant (AidData coordinates), near Qadirabad

lenders.name: Bank of China, ICBC, China Construction Bank and Agricultural Bank of China
lenders.role: US$1.44 billion syndicated buyer's credit, committed October 2015; AidData assumes equal shares of US$360 million (AidData 92302).

cases.conditions: Financed at 75:25 debt to equity, on a project cost of US$1.808 billion (some sources say US$1.912 billion), built under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. Construction ran from 31 July 2015 to 28 October 2017 (AidData).

companies.name: Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Pakistan) Energy
companies.role: Project company owned by Huaneng Shandong Power Generation (51%) and Shandong Ruyi (49%) (AidData)

cases.community: Residents say the water table fell by up to 15 feet in three to four years; the plant needs about 60,000 cubic metres of water a day. A University of Agriculture Faisalabad team took up to 220 samples, with arsenic above the WHO limit in about 45% (preliminary data). A farmer says the plant's floodlights destroy his maize, and another that 80% of his guava trees are drying, which he blames on ash. A medical camp in October 2019 reported a significant rise in breathing problems (Dawn, 2019).
cases.outcome: The prime minister's climate adviser urged the Punjab environment department to enforce the impact assessment and national standards. Promised clean water, a hospital and gas were not provided, residents say (Dawn).

sources.title: Life under the shadow of a coal-fired power plant
[CPEC] Bank of China contributes to $1.44 billion syndicated buyer's credit for Sahiwal (record 92302)

cases.confidence_note: The plant's EIA director says it never broke national standards. The water sampling is preliminary, and arsenic was not shown to come from the plant. Crop and water losses are residents' accounts. Land taking is left out of the harm above because it came before the money: villagers describe police raids and pressure over land in 2014, and one man a police case with terrorism clauses, while the loan came in October 2015. The deputy commissioner denies coercion and says compensation was generous (Dawn).

lvwhy.project: The loan built the plant that draws the groundwater.

cases.title: Nam Ou Dam Cascade: Families Moved Without Farmland
cases.point: Khoua district, near the Nam Ou 4 resettlement site, approximate

lenders.name: China Development Bank
lenders.role: US$660 million for Phase 1 (Nam Ou 2, 5, 6), signed 27 September 2013 (AidData 63762), and US$770 million of a US$1.3 billion syndicated loan for Phase 2 (Nam Ou 1, 3, 4, 7), committed 8 September 2016 (AidData 67486).

lenders.name: China Eximbank and China Construction Bank
lenders.role: Together US$530 million of Phase 2 (AidData 67486).

lenders.name: Sinosure
lenders.role: Insured the buyer's credit on both phases (AidData).

cases.conditions: Build-operate-transfer dams with Sinosure-insured loans. PowerChina Resources is the main owner (AidData).

companies.name: PowerChina Resources / Sinohydro
companies.role: Owner and builder of the cascade (AidData; RFA)

cases.community: About 1,400 people from 297 households in five villages moved on 14 March 2019 for Nam Ou 4, receiving US$350–600 per family and a year's rice; the resettlement village's vice chief said they got houses "but no land to cultivate" (RFA). At Nam Ou 1, 134 families were moved. Several hundred families moved from five villages in Ngoy district. At Nam Ou 7, more than 200 families waited for land compensation. Teak trees were paid at US$0.60–1.20 each. Generator tests at Nam Ou 4 flooded gardens and farms of about 20 families (RFA, 2020).
cases.ecosystem: International Rivers says the two northernmost dams would flood part of the Phou Den Din protected area and that the river holds over 84 fish species, 29 of them found only there; this is its expectation, not a measured loss.
cases.displaced_note: Nam Ou 4 only (RFA). Other dams moved further families; International Rivers expected 89 villages to be displaced.
cases.outcome: A Nam Ou 4 consortium representative said all villagers were paid under agreed terms. A Khoua district official said arrangements were not done yet, and RFA reports he said difficulties should be temporary. Phase 2 was completed on 29 September 2021 (RFA; AidData).

cases.title: Colombo Port City: Sand Dredging and Negombo's Fishers

lenders.name: China Development Bank
lenders.role: Agreed in principle on 16 September 2014, when the project formally started. US$805 million loan to CHEC Port City Colombo committed 12 May 2017, backed by Sinosure with no sovereign guarantee; RMB 1.964 billion paid out by September 2018 (AidData 33431). US$100 million more in April 2019 for a tunnel and access road (AidData 96170).

lenders.name: China Communications Construction Company (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Owner of the project company from the start of work in 2014 (AidData).

cases.conditions: Phase 1 built a 269-hectare artificial island on a build-own-operate-transfer basis, with 70:30 debt to equity. Reclamation of the 269 hectares was reported finished on 16 January 2019 (AidData).

companies.name: CHEC Port City Colombo / China Communications Construction Company
companies.role: Owner and borrower, a CCCC subsidiary; China Harbour was contractor (AidData)

cases.community: The company says it needed 65 million cubic metres of sand; fishers say it came from Basiyawatta in Negombo and Uswetakeiyawa in Wattala. Fishers report dredging for about three years, much lower catches and no place to launch boats. In the peak months of late 2018 a Pitipana fisher says the beach eroded about 20 metres inland in two days; about 50 families moved out for a time and ten houses were completely damaged. Some families received only about Rs. 5,000 (Daily Mirror, 2020).
cases.outcome: After a legal challenge by the All-Ceylon Fisherfolk Trade Unions, whose president says residents sought a court order in 2017, the company granted a Rs. 550 million livelihood package; about Rs. 150 million went to 75 fishery bodies, and the rest to community projects. Income support ended in July 2019 (Daily Mirror).

sources.title: Negombo fishermen hit by Port City Project
China Development Bank provides $805 million loan for Colombo Port City Project Phase 1 (record 33431)
China Development Bank provides $100 million interest-free loan for Colombo Port City Project (record 96170)

cases.confidence_note: The Coast Conservation Department blames 2018 storms and calls the Port City link a hypothesis. The Marine Environment Protection Authority says the link has not been scientifically proven. The company calls the grant a community programme. Timing: the Chinese owner was present from 2014, and the bank loan was committed in 2017 and being paid out before the late-2018 erosion; earlier catch losses came before the 2017 loan but under the same owner.

lvwhy.finance: China Development Bank funded Phase 1 and the access road.

cases.title: Hwange Units 7 and 8: Ingagula Residents and the Delayed Relocation

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: US$997.7 million preferential buyer's credit signed 1 December 2015; first US$200 million paid out in June 2018 (AidData 63475).

cases.conditions: The expansion doubled the station from 600 MW to 1,200 MW, on-lent to the project company and repaid from power sales (AidData).

companies.name: Sinohydro
companies.role: Main contractor and 36% shareholder in the project company HESCO (AidData)

cases.community: The environment agency EMA tested the air in Ingagula from 10 to 16 September 2024 and found levels significantly above Zimbabwean and WHO standards; no figures were published, and the suburb is 600 metres from the auxiliary boiler site (Bulawayo24; NewsDay). In May 2021 the site manager said more than 400 Ingagula households had to move to avoid air pollution, at more than US$60 million not in the project budget (CITE; The Standard). More than 400 residents protested the delay (The Standard). Residents and workers, through Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights, said air quality had worsened and illness was growing since the new units started (CITE, 2024).
cases.displaced_note: No completed count found. The figure was more than 400 households in 2021 and 500 in November 2024, per the Hwange Town Council spokesperson (Zimbabwe Independent summary). EMA said in 2024 that ZPC had moved "the most valuable part of Ingagula" (Zim Now).
cases.outcome: EMA asked the power company in June 2023 to reduce dust from the expansion works (NewsDay). In October 2023 ZPC and residents agreed on relocation, and ZPC committed to a site 10 km away and acknowledged the emissions' harmful effect (Bulawayo24). EMA says relocating the nearest downwind community was a condition of the project's impact assessment (Zim Now). The lawyers say EMA has not released that assessment (NewsDay).

cases.title: Karuma Dam: Evictions at Awoo and Unpaid Compensation

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Financed the US$1.7 billion, 600 MW plant (The Independent, Uganda; Just Finance International).

cases.conditions: Uganda began repaying the loan before the plant produced power (Just Finance International).

companies.name: Sinohydro
companies.role: State-owned builder of the dam and three transmission lines, from 2013

cases.community: Construction displaced more than 200 households from Karuma Town Council and 60 from the Awoo villages, and over 300 people were still unpaid about six years later (The Independent). cases.title: Tenke Fungurume Under CMOC: Sulphur Dioxide and Moves Around the 30K Plant

lenders.name: CMOC Group (China) (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Foreign owner running the mine when the harm happened: controlled it from 2016 and owns 80% of Tenke Fungurume Mining, with Gécamines holding 20% (EIA; Business & Human Rights Resource Centre).

lenders.name: Bank of China, China CITIC Bank, China Minsheng Bank and China Development Bank
lenders.role: US$1.59 billion syndicated loan signed 15 November 2016 helped CMOC buy 56% of the mine for US$2.65 billion. Scheduled repayment ended in November 2023 (AidData 91890). It paid for the purchase, not the 30K plant, and AidData does not say whether it was repaid or refinanced.

cases.conditions: The loan financed the purchase of the mine from Freeport-McMoRan, secured on CMOC's stake in its holding company (AidData).

companies.name: CMOC Group
companies.role: Owner and operator through Tenke Fungurume Mining

cases.community: The Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) and PremiCongo report large sulphur dioxide releases since the 30K processing plant opened in 2023. Monitoring they commissioned recorded above 0.7 parts per million for about 40 minutes on 28 September 2024 and above 0.5 for several hours in December 2024 in the Manomapia neighbourhood; the WHO 10-minute guideline is 0.191 (EIA). More than 1,200 clinic records show rising nosebleeds, coughing and vomiting of blood; the report also cites pregnancy complications including stillbirths (EIA; Down To Earth, 2026). In May 2024 the company agreed to move and compensate more than 1,000 families (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre).
cases.displaced_note: More than 12,000 since 2022, per EIA: about 3,000 at Kabombwa (2024), 4,498 at Kalweji (2022–23; RAID gives 4,289 for the Kibalasani–Kalweji road) and about 5,000 at Manomapia (2024–25; TFM says about 1,500 families). EIA's own press release says more than 10,000. All fall under CMOC's ownership. TFM says it supported relocations and gives no total.
cases.outcome: In March 2026 nine civil society groups called for an end to the pollution, independent monitoring and fair compensation (RAID). On 25 March 2026 the Congolese government announced an inspection of the mine (News Ghana; EnviroNews Nigeria).

cases.title: Kenya SGR Phase 2A: Blasting Damage at Twala and the Nairobi National Park Viaduct
cases.place: Nairobi National Park and Twala, Kajiado, Kenya
cases.point: Nairobi National Park, where the viaduct crosses; Twala in Kajiado could not be pinned down

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: US$1.39 billion buyer's credit signed 3 December 2015 for the 120 km Nairobi–Naivasha line, financing 85% of the contract, insured by Sinosure. In April 2018 the bank reportedly withheld KES 32 billion because of court cases (AidData 47025).

cases.conditions: The Kenyan government borrowed and on-lent to Kenya Railways, with the debt secured on Railway Development Fund revenue held in escrow (AidData).
cases.community: In 2017 a Chinese company building the line used explosives to break rock at Milimani in Twala, cracking houses and destroying foundations of some still being built, according to the 22 families who sued and have been in court since 2020 (Kenyans.co.ke, 2025).
cases.ecosystem: A 6.5 km viaduct crosses Nairobi National Park (AidData). Conservationists said building in the park went ahead in defiance of a court order (AFP via The EastAfrican, 2018). No measured damage to the park was found.
cases.outcome: On 10 February 2025 the Land and Environment Court at Kajiado ordered Ksh32 million in compensation for the 22 families; the company gave notice of appeal days later. The line opened on 16 October 2019 (Kenyans.co.ke; AidData).

cases.title: Chancay Megaport: Fishers' Grounds and Houses Damaged by a Tunnel Landslide

lenders.name: COSCO Shipping Ports (China) (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Majority owner of the port: 60%, with Volcan of Peru holding 40% (Lex Latin; AidData).

lenders.name: Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Minsheng Banking Corp. and Shanghai Rural Commercial Bank
lenders.role: US$975 million, 15-year syndicated loan for Phase 1 of the US$1.3 billion port, closed 28 March 2023 (Lex Latin; AidData 99565; Bloomberg via AJOT).

cases.conditions: Debt financing for a port with a dredged 17-metre (56-foot) shipping channel, a breakwater and a 1.8 km tunnel under a residential area (AP; Reuters via Datamar).
cases.community: A landslide on 16 May 2023 at the port's tunnel site damaged at least four houses, and work stopped (Reuters via Datamar). Fishers say dredging ruined breeding grounds and report losing fishing spots, with one saying he needs a bigger boat to reach fish. Locals say the breakwater changed currents, hurting ice sellers, truckers and restaurants (AP, 2024).
cases.outcome: Peru's prosecutor opened a preliminary investigation after the landslide. COSCO manager Mario de las Casas said the company has begun studies on how the port could reduce inequality and spur local growth (Reuters via Datamar; AP).
